blocks.body:
A random variable is described by a whole list of numbers: the probabilities $P(X = 0), P(X = 1), P(X = 2), \dots$, or a density. Adding independent random variables means convolving such lists, which is clumsy. The trick of this page is to package the whole distribution into a single function. Adding independent variables then becomes multiplying functions, and moments such as the mean and variance fall out by differentiating.

There are two versions. The probability generating function (PGF) is made for variables taking values $0, 1, 2, \dots$ and is exactly an ordinary [[generating-functions|generating function]] whose coefficients are probabilities. The moment generating function (MGF) works for any real random variable and has the moments $E[X^n]$ as its [[taylor|Taylor coefficients]] (up to factorials). Both rest on [[random-variables|expectation]] and on [[power-series]].

blocks.title: Probability and moment generating functions
blocks.body:
Let $X$ take values in $\{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ with $p_k = P(X = k)$. Its probability generating function is
$$G_X(s) = E\left[s^X\right] = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} p_k s^k .$$
For any real random variable $X$, its moment generating function is
$$M_X(t) = E\left[e^{tX}\right],$$
defined for those real $t$ where the expectation is finite. We say $X$ has an MGF when $M_X(t)$ is finite for all $t$ in some open interval $(-h, h)$ with $h > 0$.

The PGF is a power series with nonnegative coefficients summing to $1$, so it converges at least for $|s| \le 1$ and $G_X(1) = 1$. For such $X$ the two functions are related by $M_X(t) = G_X(e^t)$.

blocks.title: The PGF: a distribution as a polynomial
blocks.body:
Take a fair six-sided die. Its PGF is
$$G(s) = \tfrac16\left(s + s^2 + s^3 + s^4 + s^5 + s^6\right).$$
Nothing has been lost: the coefficient of $s^k$ is $P(X = k)$, and in general $p_k = G^{(k)}(0)/k!$, so the PGF determines the distribution.

Now differentiate. Since $G'(s) = \sum k p_k s^{k-1}$, setting $s = 1$ gives $G'(1) = \sum k p_k = E[X]$. Differentiating again, $G''(1) = \sum k(k-1)p_k = E[X(X-1)]$, the second factorial moment. Hence
$$E[X] = G'(1), \qquad \operatorname{Var}(X) = G''(1) + G'(1) - G'(1)^2 .$$
For the die, $G'(1) = 21/6 = 7/2$ and $G''(1) = 70/6 = 35/3$, so $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 35/3 + 7/2 - 49/4 = 35/12$. (When $X$ has infinite mean, $G'(s) \to \infty$ as $s \to 1^-$; the formulas are read as limits from the left.)

The main reason to use a PGF is sums. If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then so are $s^X$ and $s^Y$, and the expectation of a product of independent variables is the product of the expectations:
$$G_{X+Y}(s) = E\left[s^X s^Y\right] = E\left[s^X\right] E\left[s^Y\right] = G_X(s)\,G_Y(s).$$
Multiplying the polynomials automatically performs the convolution $P(X + Y = n) = \sum_k P(X = k)P(Y = n-k)$.

Some standard PGFs, with $q = 1 - p$:

- Bernoulli($p$): $q + ps$. So Binomial($n, p$), a sum of $n$ independent Bernoullis, has $G(s) = (q + ps)^n$.
- Poisson($\lambda$): $\sum e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k s^k/k! = e^{\lambda(s-1)}$.
- Geometric($p$) on $\{1, 2, \dots\}$ (the number of trials up to and including the first success): $G(s) = \dfrac{ps}{1 - qs}$ for $|s| < 1/q$.

From $(q + ps)^n$ we get $G'(1) = np$ and $G''(1) = n(n-1)p^2$, so the variance is $n(n-1)p^2 + np - n^2p^2 = np(1-p)$, with no binomial-coefficient juggling at all.

blocks.title: The MGF: moments as Taylor coefficients
blocks.body:
For a variable with a density, or one taking negative or non-integer values, $s^X$ is awkward, so we write $s = e^t$ and use $M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}]$. Expanding the exponential,
$$M_X(t) = E\left[\sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{t^n X^n}{n!}\right] = \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{E[X^n]}{n!}\, t^n ,$$
and when $M_X$ is finite on an interval $(-h, h)$ this exchange of sum and expectation is justified, $M_X$ is a convergent power series there, and
$$M_X^{(n)}(0) = E\left[X^n\right].$$
That is the origin of the name: the MGF generates the moments.

Two examples worth knowing. If $X$ is exponential with rate $\lambda$, then $M_X(t) = \int_0^\infty e^{tx}\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\,dx = \dfrac{\lambda}{\lambda - t}$ for $t < \lambda$ (and $M_X(t) = \infty$ for $t \ge \lambda$). Expanding $1/(1 - t/\lambda) = \sum t^n/\lambda^n$ shows at once that $E[X^n] = n!/\lambda^n$. If $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$, completing the square in the integral gives $M_X(t) = e^{\mu t + \sigma^2 t^2/2}$ for all $t$.

Two rules do most of the work: $M_{aX + b}(t) = e^{bt} M_X(at)$, and $M_{X+Y} = M_X M_Y$ when $X, Y$ are independent (same proof as for PGFs). For example, if $X \sim N(\mu_1, \sigma_1^2)$ and $Y \sim N(\mu_2, \sigma_2^2)$ are independent, the product of their MGFs is $e^{(\mu_1 + \mu_2)t + (\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2)t^2/2}$, the MGF of $N(\mu_1 + \mu_2, \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2)$. To conclude that $X + Y$ really has that distribution we need the next theorem.

blocks.title: Uniqueness and the product rule
blocks.body:
1. (PGFs) If $G_X(s) = G_Y(s)$ for all $s$ in some interval $[0, \varepsilon)$ with $\varepsilon > 0$, then $X$ and $Y$ have the same distribution.
2. (MGFs) If $M_X(t)$ and $M_Y(t)$ are both finite and equal for all $t$ in an open interval $(-h, h)$, $h > 0$, then $X$ and $Y$ have the same distribution.
3. (Sums) If $X_1, \dots, X_n$ are independent, then $G_{X_1 + \cdots + X_n} = \prod G_{X_i}$ and $M_{X_1 + \cdots + X_n} = \prod M_{X_i}$ wherever the factors are finite.

blocks.title: Proof of parts 1 and 3
blocks.body:
Part 1: $G_X$ and $G_Y$ are power series converging on $(-1, 1)$, and two power series that agree on $[0, \varepsilon)$ have the same coefficients, because the $k$th coefficient equals $G^{(k)}(0)/k!$ and the derivatives at $0$ can be computed using only values on $[0, \varepsilon)$ (one-sided limits of difference quotients). So $P(X = k) = P(Y = k)$ for every $k$.

Part 3: the variables $s^{X_i}$ (or $e^{tX_i}$) are independent and nonnegative, and for independent nonnegative variables $E[\prod Z_i] = \prod E[Z_i]$, so the expectation of the product of $s^{X_i}$ factorises.

Part 2 is genuinely deeper: it is an inversion theorem for the Laplace transform, or, extending $t$ to complex values, for the Fourier transform (the characteristic function). We use it without proof; see the references.

blocks.title: Random sums: composition of PGFs
blocks.body:
A common model: a random number $N$ of customers arrive, and customer $i$ spends $X_i$, with the $X_i$ independent, identically distributed and independent of $N$. The total $S = X_1 + \cdots + X_N$ (with $S = 0$ if $N = 0$) is a random sum. Conditioning on $N$,
$$G_S(s) = E\left[E\left[s^S \mid N\right]\right] = E\left[G_X(s)^N\right] = G_N\big(G_X(s)\big).$$
So the PGF of a random sum is a composition. Differentiating with the chain rule at $s = 1$ (where $G_X(1) = 1$) gives $E[S] = G_N'(1)\,G_X'(1) = E[N]\,E[X]$, which is intuitive; the variance formula $\operatorname{Var}(S) = E[N]\operatorname{Var}(X) + \operatorname{Var}(N)E[X]^2$ follows from the second derivative. The same composition rule drives branching processes: if each individual has offspring with PGF $G$, the size of generation $n$ has PGF $G \circ G \circ \cdots \circ G$ ($n$ times).

blocks.title: Tail bounds and the characteristic function
blocks.body:
MGFs also give tail bounds. For any $t > 0$, the event $X \ge a$ is the event $e^{tX} \ge e^{ta}$, so Markov's inequality gives
$$P(X \ge a) \le e^{-ta} M_X(t), \qquad \text{hence} \qquad P(X \ge a) \le \inf_{t > 0} e^{-ta} M_X(t).$$
This is the Chernoff bound. For $X \sim \text{Binomial}(100, 1/2)$ and $a = 75$, minimising $e^{-75t}\left(\frac{1 + e^t}{2}\right)^{100}$ gives $e^t = 3$ and the bound $\approx 2.1 \times 10^{-6}$; the true probability is about $2.8 \times 10^{-7}$. Chebyshev's inequality would only give a bound of about $0.04$ for this event, so the exponential bound is enormously better. The bound equals $e^{-100D}$ with $D = \tfrac34 \ln \tfrac32 + \tfrac14 \ln \tfrac12 \approx 0.131$, the relative [[entropy]] (in nats) of a coin with bias $3/4$ from a fair coin.

The MGF has one weakness: it may not exist. For the Cauchy distribution, or any distribution with a heavy tail such as a density proportional to $1/x^3$ for large $x$, $E[e^{tX}] = \infty$ for every $t > 0$. The fix is the characteristic function $\varphi_X(t) = E[e^{itX}]$, which is finite for every random variable because $|e^{itX}| = 1$. It has the same product rule and uniqueness property, and Lévy's continuity theorem (stated here without proof) says that if $\varphi_{X_n}(t) \to \varphi_X(t)$ for every $t$ then $X_n \to X$ in distribution. When MGFs exist on a common interval around $0$, the analogous statement for MGFs also holds (again without proof here), and this is the standard route to the central limit theorem in [[limit-theorems]].
Use PGFs to find the distribution of the total $T$ of two fair dice, then its mean and variance.
blocks.solution:
By the product rule, $G_T(s) = G(s)^2 = \frac{1}{36}\left(s + \cdots + s^6\right)^2$. Expanding,
$$G_T(s) = \tfrac{1}{36}\left(s^2 + 2s^3 + 3s^4 + 4s^5 + 5s^6 + 6s^7 + 5s^8 + 4s^9 + 3s^{10} + 2s^{11} + s^{12}\right),$$
so for instance $P(T = 7) = 6/36 = 1/6$.

For the moments, differentiate $G_T = G^2$: $G_T' = 2GG'$, so $G_T'(1) = 2 \cdot 1 \cdot \tfrac72 = 7$. Then $G_T'' = 2(G')^2 + 2GG''$, so $G_T''(1) = 2 \cdot \tfrac{49}{4} + 2 \cdot \tfrac{35}{3} = \tfrac{287}{6}$. Hence
$$\operatorname{Var}(T) = \tfrac{287}{6} + 7 - 49 = \tfrac{35}{6},$$
twice the variance $35/12$ of one die, as it must be for independent summands.

blocks.body: A hen lays $N \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)$ eggs, and each egg independently hatches with probability $p$. Find the distribution of the number $H$ of chicks.
blocks.solution:
$H$ is a random sum of $N$ independent Bernoulli($p$) variables, independent of $N$, so
$$G_H(s) = G_N\big(G_X(s)\big) = e^{\lambda\left((q + ps) - 1\right)} = e^{\lambda p (s - 1)} .$$
This is the PGF of Poisson($\lambda p$), so by uniqueness $H \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda p)$. Thinning a Poisson count keeps it Poisson.

blocks.body: Can two six-sided dice be loaded (each face of each die given some probability, the two dice rolled independently) so that the total is equally likely to be each of $2, 3, \dots, 12$?
blocks.solution:
No. Suppose die A shows $k$ with probability $a_k$ and die B with probability $b_k$. The total would have to have PGF
$$G_A(s)G_B(s) = \tfrac{1}{11}\left(s^2 + s^3 + \cdots + s^{12}\right).$$
Comparing the coefficients of $s^2$ and $s^{12}$, $a_1 b_1 = a_6 b_6 = 1/11$, so $a_1, a_6, b_1, b_6$ are all positive. Write $G_A(s) = s\,A(s)$ with $A(s) = a_1 + a_2 s + \cdots + a_6 s^5$, and similarly $G_B(s) = s\,B(s)$. Since $a_6 > 0$, $A$ is a real polynomial of odd degree $5$, so it has a real root $r$; then
$$A(r)B(r) = \tfrac{1}{11}\left(1 + r + \cdots + r^{10}\right) = 0.$$
But $1 + r + \cdots + r^{10}$ has no real root: at $r = 1$ it equals $11$, and for $r \ne 1$ it equals $(r^{11} - 1)/(r - 1)$, which vanishes only if $r^{11} = 1$, impossible for real $r \ne 1$. Contradiction.

The same factorisation idea shows what is possible. The "Sicherman dice" with faces $1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4$ and $1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8$ satisfy
$$\left(s + 2s^2 + 2s^3 + s^4\right)\left(s + s^3 + s^4 + s^5 + s^6 + s^8\right) = \left(s + s^2 + \cdots + s^6\right)^2,$$
so they give exactly the same distribution of totals as two ordinary dice; they come from regrouping the irreducible factors $s$, $1 + s$, $1 + s + s^2$, $1 - s + s^2$ of $s + \cdots + s^6$.

blocks.body:
- The PGF is only for variables with values in $\{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$. For other variables use the MGF or the characteristic function.
- Uniqueness of MGFs needs $M_X$ finite on an open interval around $0$. A function finite only at $t = 0$ (Cauchy, or any heavy-tailed law) tells you nothing.
- Knowing all the moments $E[X^n]$ does not, in general, determine a distribution: the lognormal distribution has the same moments as other, different distributions, and its MGF is infinite for every $t > 0$. Moments determine the law when the MGF exists near $0$.
- $M_{X+Y} = M_X M_Y$ needs independence (uncorrelated is not enough). For $Y = X$ we get $M_{2X}(t) = M_X(2t)$, not $M_X(t)^2$.
- In the random-sum formula $G_N(G_X(s))$ the order matters, and $N$ must be independent of the $X_i$.

The PGF is the probabilistic face of [[generating-functions]]: counting problems often become probability problems by normalising coefficients, and vice versa. The MGF is a two-sided Laplace transform (compare [[laplace-transform]]), and the characteristic function is a [[fourier-transform]] of the distribution; the product rule for sums is the convolution theorem. MGFs and characteristic functions give the cleanest proofs in [[limit-theorems]], Chernoff bounds are a workhorse of the [[probabilistic-method]], and the logarithm $\ln M_X(t)$ (the cumulant generating function) is the bridge to large deviations and to [[entropy]]. In [[markov-chains]] and branching processes, iterated PGFs compute extinction probabilities.

1. A fair tetrahedral die has faces $1, 2, 3, 4$. Write down its PGF and use it to find the probability that the total of three such dice is $6$.
2. A random variable has MGF $M(t) = (1 - 2t)^{-3}$ for $t < 1/2$. Find its mean and variance.
3. Show that the sum of $n$ independent Geometric($p$) variables on $\{1, 2, \dots\}$ has PGF $\left(\dfrac{ps}{1 - qs}\right)^n$, and deduce its mean.
4. If $N \sim \text{Geometric}(p)$ on $\{1, 2, \dots\}$ and the $X_i$ are independent Poisson($\mu$), independent of $N$, find $E[S]$ and $\operatorname{Var}(S)$ for $S = X_1 + \cdots + X_N$.
